paragraphs: Things are different for ordinary people. They have little time for education. Their parents can hardly afford to look after them, even when they are babies. As soon as the children are able to work, they must learn a trade so that they can earn a living. This trade is usually so simple and repetitive that it gives the mind very little exercise. At the same time, their work is so constant and so hard that it leaves them little free time. It also leaves them even less desire to study anything else, or even to think about it.

In any civilized society, ordinary people cannot be as well educated as people with a high position and money. However, the most essential parts of education are reading, writing and arithmetic. Children can learn these skills so early in life that most of them have time to learn them before they start working. This is true even for those who will do the lowest jobs. For a very small cost, the state can make this easier for almost all the people. It can also encourage them, and it can even make it compulsory.

The state can make it easier by opening a small school in every parish or district. There, children can learn for a very low fee. Even an ordinary labourer can pay it. The teacher should be paid partly by the state, but not completely. If the state paid all or even most of his salary, he would soon learn to neglect his work. In Scotland, these parish schools have taught almost all ordinary people to read, and a large number of them to write and do arithmetic. In England, charity schools have had a similar effect, but less widely, because there are not as many of them. The books used in these schools could be a little more instructive than they usually are. Also, the children of ordinary people sometimes learn a little Latin there, which is almost never useful to them. If they learned the basic parts of geometry and mechanics instead, the education of this class of people would perhaps be as complete as it can be. There is hardly any ordinary trade that does not offer some chances to use the principles of geometry and mechanics. So these trades would slowly train ordinary people in those principles. And these principles are the necessary introduction to the highest and also the most useful sciences.
The state can encourage people to learn these essential skills by giving small prizes and little badges of honour to the children of ordinary people who do well in them.

Finally, the state can make almost everyone learn these essential skills. It can do this by making every man pass an examination in them before he can become a member of a trade guild. Without this examination, he would not be allowed to start a business, either in a village or in a town.
